newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: FEATURE - Botswana peers beyond sparkling diamonds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Botswana peers beyond sparkling diamonds.

text.p: On a continent of grinding poverty and political upheaval, Botswana is a rare island of stability and prosperity.
Since independence in 1966, this vast but sparsely populated southern African state, once the third poorest in the world, has built a fine infrastructure of roads and schools.
It has also stashed away $5 billion in foreign reserves -- $3,300 for every man, woman and child -- thanks to diamonds.
Botswana is the world's largest producer of gem-quality diamonds and impressive new buildings on the Gaborone skyline attest to buoyant demand for its gems from New York to Tokyo.
But diamond wealth does not spell jobs and the government is under pressure to address the country's biggest problem -- unemployment -- by stimulating economic diversification.
DIAMOND-BACKED

At present, the economy rests on the backs of 6,000 diamond miners whose output accounts for 80 percent of export earnings and a third of gross domestic product. It also depends on the survival of the De Beers Central Selling Organisation (CSO) cartel which controls the market.
For now the diamond outlook looks bright.

Prices are up after a worrying wobble in the early 1990s, raising hopes that Botswana's CSO quota may be increased next year. At the same time a new agreement with the unions for continuous working will increase output by some 15 percent.
More significantly, diamond producer Debswana, owned jointly by De Beers and the state, plans to expand its Orapa mine, lifting national output to 23 million carats from 17 million by 2000.
That will ensure accelerating growth by the end of the decade, said vice-president and finance minister Festus Mogae.
EXTRA SPARKLE

He expects the economy to expand by an average of around five percent a year over the course of the 1997-2003 development plan, due to be unveiled early next year, up from initial projections of 4.7 percent.
"The Orapa expansion means that when we look at the figures again we should be expecting somewhat higher growth, especially towards to the end of the period," Mogae told Reuters.
"We could see growth of six or seven percent three or four years from now, maybe more."
That is impressive by comparison with estimated growth of 3.1 percent in 1995/96 (July-June), but diamond growth alone will not deal with unemployment estimated at 23-25 percent.
After 30 years of prudent management of diamond revenues Botswana is entering a new era, according to business leaders.

"We've got to a watershed. The government has developed the economy as far as it can by building infrastructure. The risk is continued government intervention will start to stifle the private sector," said Stockbrokers Botswana chief executive Alan Norrie.
NOW FOR THE JOBS
"The question is now how to get the private sector to develop and create sustainable wealth-generating employment -- and it's not easy."

A start has been made on diversification, and a nascent manufacturing industry is taking shape, most notably with the Hyundai car assembly plant in Gaborone, which is exporting heavily to South Africa.
Foreign textile firms are also being encouraged and the government is working on legislation designed to encourage the development of financial services.
But it is an uphill struggle, not least with the re-emergence of South Africa as a viable competing location for capital investment after years of sanctions.
One way or another it is the private sector which must drive the economy into the next century, according to central Bank of Bostwana research director Jay Salkin:
"More growth has to come from outside government."
The challenge to create jobs through diversification is likely to be the key issue in the next elections, due by 1999.
The Botswana Democratic Party has ruled since independence but the political landscape is changing, too, with President Ketumile Masire, who has ruled since 1980, planning to retire.

And the opposition Botswana National Front is starting to flex its muscles after increasing its representation from three to 13 in the 40-seat parliament in the 1994 elections, campaigning on a ticket highlighting unemployment.
